name: neurosync-contradiction-eval
description: Curated, human-authored labeled examples for measuring NeuroSync's rule-based contradiction detection. Every example is a pair of short source texts that are fed through the real claim-extraction and conflict-detection code paths. Labels are ground truth authored independently of the detector's output.

label_definition.label_true: The two sources make incompatible assertions about the same subject and property (same property, contemporaneous or no legitimate differentiator), so they cannot both be accurate. This is the positive class.
label_definition.label_false: The two sources are compatible, equivalent after unit normalisation, refer to different times (so a difference may be a genuine change), lack the context to compare, or carry insufficient information to contradict. This is the negative class.
label_definition.expected_flagged: Whether the detector is expected to surface *any* conflict (including the softer temporal_inconsistency and missing_context signals that are not themselves confirmed contradictions).
label_definition.expected_types: The conflict_type value(s) the detector should assign. Any one of these counts as a correct classification for reporting.

notes: Texts use a fixed neutral date/time format (e.g. '10:00 AM') that the deterministic extractor parses without a calendar date.

Source reliability is recorded in 'source_a_reliability'/'source_b_reliability' for documentation only; the pairwise detector deliberately ignores reliability (it is applied later, in evidence scoring).
These are synthetic, clearly-labelled evaluation fixtures and are never loaded into a production database.

examples.rationale: 100°F is 37.8°C, which differs from 40°C by more than the 2% tolerance, so these are incompatible temperature readings of the same subject at the same time.
104°F is 40°C, which contradicts 30°C for the same subject at the same time after unit conversion.
100°F equals 37.8°C within rounding; the readings agree once units are normalised, so this is not a contradiction.

examples.text_a: The pressure reading was 5 kPa at 10:00 AM.
examples.text_b: The pressure reading was 5 bar at 10:00 AM.
examples.rationale: kPa and bar are related but the detector only converts temperature; it cannot confirm a value clash, so it correctly flags missing unit context rather than asserting a contradiction.

examples.text_a: The flow was 5 L/min at 10:00 AM.
examples.text_b: The flow was 5 kg at 10:00 AM.
examples.rationale: L/min (volume flow) and kg (mass) are different physical dimensions and are not convertible, so the values cannot be compared without context.

examples.text_a: Machine M-17 temperature was 92°C at 10:00 AM.
examples.text_b: Machine M-17 temperature was 76°C at 11:30 AM.
examples.rationale: Readings 90 minutes apart exceeding the 30-minute gap threshold may reflect a genuine change over time, so this is surfaced for investigation but is not a confirmed contemporaneous contradiction.
Three hours apart and above the gap threshold; the difference may be a genuine trend rather than a contradiction.
The values agree, so there is nothing to flag regardless of the time gap.
A 20-minute gap is below the 30-minute threshold, so the large difference is treated as a contemporaneous contradiction rather than a possible trend.
Same value and within the gap threshold; nothing to flag.
Only one report records a time, so it is unclear whether the differing readings are contemporaneous; the detector flags missing time context rather than asserting a contradiction.
Neither report records a time, so there is no temporal differentiator and the large difference is a contemporaneous disagreement (a contradiction).

examples.text_a: The vibration was 5 mm/s at 10:00 AM.
examples.text_b: The vibration was 5 mm at 10:00 AM.
examples.rationale: mm/s (velocity) and mm (displacement) are different dimensions; comparison needs context.

examples.text_a: Machine M-17 reached a temperature of 92°C during inspection at 10:00 AM.
examples.text_b: Machine M-17 reached a temperature of 76°C during inspection at 10:00 AM.
examples.rationale: Two documents report different temperatures for the same machine at the same time; a direct contradiction.
A very large contemporaneous difference (>25%) between two documents; a clear contradiction.

examples.text_a: The machine was observed operating normally.
examples.text_b: The machine was observed not operating normally.
examples.rationale: One report affirms and the other negates the same observed state; directly opposed assertions.
Both reports assert a status for the same subject but disagree on the value; a semantic inconsistency.
A low-reliability source reporting an outlier still contradicts the reliable reading; the detector should flag it and let evidence scoring down-weight the unreliable source.
Two low-reliability sources still contradict each other; detection is independent of reliability, which is applied downstream.
The low-reliability source agrees with the reliable one, so there is no contradiction to flag.
Consistent values, no contradiction.

examples.text_b: The maintenance team met on Tuesday to discuss the schedule.
examples.rationale: The second text contains no structured claim, so there is insufficient information to establish a contradiction.
Neither text yields a comparable subject/property claim; nothing can be contradicted.
Only one source provides evidence; a single observation cannot contradict itself.

examples.text_b: The pressure was 5 kPa at 10:00 AM.
examples.rationale: Different properties of different quantities are different facts, not a contradiction.

examples.text_b: A temperature of 92°C was recorded at 10:00 AM.
examples.rationale: The same fact expressed in different words; equivalent, not contradictory.

examples.text_b: At 10:00 AM the temperature reading was 92°C.
examples.rationale: Reordered clause, identical meaning; equivalent.
Equivalent statements that use different units; must not be reported as a contradiction.
A 0.8% difference is within the 2% tolerance and is treated as measurement agreement, not a contradiction.

Hard case: 'temp' and 'temperature' denote the same property, so the same-time readings genuinely contradict. The rule-based extractor maps them to different subjects and is expected to miss this (false negative).
Hard case: 'not running' opposes 'operating normally'. 'running' is not in the state/status vocabulary, so the second statement is expected to yield no claim and be missed (false negative).

examples.text_a: The machine was operating normally, with no anomalies.
examples.rationale: Hard case: both statements say the machine is normal, so there is no contradiction. The word 'no' is a negation marker, so the detector is expected to flip the first statement's polarity and raise a spurious direct_contradiction (false positive).
